2186.content:
Gauge Stones, the ring, the lock and the well are in the guide Reckoners in the world. Where the
places themselves are — The Overworld.

2187.content:
The Reckoners' library deep in the Inkpine Forest: a hall of inkstone masonry with a pale band of tile, a rose window of
scrollbark over the entrance, a bell tower with an inkwell lamp. Inside are the copyists' long table, niches of scroll shelves
under a gallery, and on the gallery a banded coffer and the "Copyist register"; in the collapsed wing is a bindery with vats
of ink. The shelves hold paper, cord, Tally Tablets, now and then a Woven Record, resin and scrollbark.

2188.content:
The **reading room** behind the north wall is locked by a seal: four rune plates lie before it out of order, and above four
niches in the walls are rune signs. The lectern at the entrance tells how to read the order: "a copy is made bay by bay, from the
door to the reading room". Step on the plates in the order of the niches. The reading room holds a sealed coffer,
a chest and a barrel of Records: Woven Records, Drive Drawings, Opaline Inclusions, Lattice and Fray shards.

2189.content:
By the path through the forest stands the **Copyist's Lodge** — an inkpine cabin with an ink press: its barrel holds resin,
scrollbark, an early Tally Tablet, a  and saplings.

2190.content:
The Reckoners kept their ledgers under a riverbed; in the Great Stopping the river was dammed, the water went into the archive
and stands there still. It is a **great dungeon**: above the water you see only the intake tower with belts of glowing marks —
at night it is girded with runes, and a beacon lantern burns on its roof.

2191.content: **The tower** is a well down to the bottom of the riverbed and below, a spiral ramp around a gauge column.

2192.content:
**Stacks and a reading room**, sunken shelves under water and walkways; the barrels of the dead ends hold paper, Records,
cord, quickdust.

2193.content:
**The counting room** is a mezzanine with rune plates: the order is the signs on the west wall from left to right; behind
a niche's seal is a banded coffer.

2194.content:
**The drain pit** is 5 × 5, five layers of water and two valves — the same puzzle as the lock, but reversed: the mark is at
the bottom.

2195.content:
**The counting hall** is a nave with galleries and a measuring pool with valves on a dais: water at the mark raises the
vault's gate. The guardian sleeps here too.

2196.content:
**The vault** holds the , two sealed coffers and a chest: chapter Records, Opaline
Inclusions, fluxsteel, antimony, shards of all six currents. It is held both by the pool's valves and by the guardian: the
vault opens when the water is solved and the guardian is down. The vault's walls are cast — no digging in.

2199.content:
The Tollkeepers are former lock keepers: they draw flux right out of the ground, and in a fight also the charge of your gear
().

2200.content:
A **Toll Post** is an old Gauge Stone with a brass **Toll Tap** driven into its side and an awning with a counting table and
scales. The ground around is drunk dry. While a player is near, the tap drains its 3 × 3 chunks to the bottom, and the
neighbors' flux flows off toward them: a workshop a few chunks from the post suddenly stands half empty — the Loupe and the
mod's notice tell you a tap is drinking the flux and where it is. **Break the tap** — what it drank goes back to the land.
Two Toll Collectors and a Bursar guard the post. Its barrel holds Toll Reliquaries, Spring shards, copper, cord and the
.

2202.content:
A  can be smashed on the ground: what was drunk pours into the chunk — that is how a dry
workshop is raised at once. Reliquaries also pay the Sluice Arch's toll to the Quickstream.

2203.content: The Sunken are former weir keepers who feed the mire and call it the Mother Below ().

2204.content:
A **Mire Shrine** stands by swamps and quiet rivers: a ring of stakes wound with mire threads around a .
The shrine's chunk is always in mire — you can see it from afar by the flakes of murk. The idol feeds murk to its chunk and
the four neighboring ones **until it is broken**. The shrine is guarded by Sodden — they rise out of the water next to you —
and a Keener whose song takes away your air: get out of her sight or knock her down mid-song. The chest holds silt, candles
and a .

2205.content:
The **Sunken Sanctum** is a Reckoner lock the Sunken took for a temple: a half-flooded dungeon on stilts in a swamp or the
Stagnant Backwater. A porch and a spiral ramp lead down into **flooded halls** with Sodden (13 blocks below the surface); the
halls hold a chest with the . Next come the rune plates of the "drowned litany" (the order is
on the lectern) and the descent to the lower lock: the gate behind the socket's seal is opened by the Drowned Keystone. Another
10 blocks down is the guardian's lake, and beyond it the treasury: diamonds, emeralds, gold, opaline, fluxsteel, Tide crystals.

2206.content: Spoiler — open the page to read

2207.content:
Fluxionists and clockmakers lived in quiet places long before you — their homes stand empty, and the journals on the lecterns
hint at what to gather there.

2208.content:
The **Clockmakers' Observatory** (Honeyfall Grove) is a round tower of umber masonry under a green copper dome, with a sundial
in the yard; its northeast side has collapsed. In the hall stands the Armillary Sphere (reading it opens the entry
), and on the gallery a Reckoner coffer, a clockmaker's journal and a barrel: honey resin, a Channel
Record, Hour Marks, a Lattice shard. Leafwights lie in the litter beyond the wall.

2209.content:
The **Fluxionist's Homestead** (Honeyfall Grove) is a two-story half-timbered house with a garden by a stream; in the lean-to
is a workshop where the Flux Workbench never woke: copper, fluxsteel, Speculum Blend, a Small Lens Blank, regulus.

2210.content:
The **Herbalist's Hut** (Sanguine Weald) is a cabin on the roots of an old aspen, four blocks above the leafmold; a ladder up
the trunk leads to the hatch. The herbalist tapped the trunk from inside the room: the chest holds heartsap, Bloom Tonics,
aspen saplings, candlecaps, now and then a Reckoner Record; the barrel holds dried herbs.

2211.content: Spoiler — open the page to read

2212.content:
The Reckoners measured the fens with weirs, and the Snaglings took them apart stone by stone: across a channel lies a row of
hewn stone with gaps, a toppled Gauge Stone, and under the water a Reckoner coffer. On the bank stands a Snagling marker of the
same stones with a wicker lantern and a barrel: paper, cord, a Tally Tablet, quickdust, silt, rods, a Tide shard.

2213.content:
On an old road in the Hourless Wood stands a caravan stopped mid-step when the Stillness tore away from the world: the front
cart under its canopy with a horse mid-step, a wheel and a fallen crate hanging in the air, and along the road stand
**Laggards** — they stand, then lunge to catch up. The front cart's chest holds grain, wool, leather, bread, a
, a , now and then a  and the Rule of the
Still Hour; the crates hold goods.

2214.content: Spoiler — open the page to read

2215.content: Villagers — the gauger with a map to the archive, the lamplighter and the herbalist.

2216.content: The Snaglings — camps, the Catch Heap and the peddler.

2218.content: Reckoners in the world — stones, Records, the lock puzzle.

2220.content: A small folk of the flux places: becoming kin with gifts to their craving, grudges and kin fights, trading and the Catch Heap, camps and the Peddler.

2229.content:
The **Snaglings** trade with those they have taken in as kin — Bolas, Catch Bundles, concentrates and opaline, Reckoner
Records and Flux Pebbles — and let their kin at the Catch Heap in the middle of the camp. They pay and take not emeralds but
**craving**: every band craves one Spring, and only things carrying that Spring are worth anything to it. They are a small,
quick folk of the places where the flux of the world runs thick and wild; you hear the dry rustle of their sedge cloaks before
you see them. Codex entry — : reading a Snagling with the Loupe opens it. Trades of every kin are in the
folk reference.

2230.content:
**The folk's home** is the Rustling Fens (places of the world): most of them live there, in **stiltholds** —
wicker huts under reed thatch on bog-oak stilts above the channels.

2231.content:
**Wandering bands** of two to four roam by day through the Weeping Floodplain, jungles,
swamps and mushroom fields. There are no Snaglings in murky chunks: to them murk is catch gone rotten.

2232.content:
**A Snagling Camp** is a clearing with three shelters, a catch pole with lanterns and a fire pit, and in the middle the
**Catch Heap**, the band's hoard. Camp dwellers do not wander far from it and sit by it at night.

2233.content: "What flows belongs to no one," the Snaglings say: a thing on the ground is **catch** to them.

2234.content:
A Snagling picks up whatever lies within 12 blocks (a Gleaner) or 6 (the others) and tosses it into its creel; a Gleaner with
a full creel carries it to the Heap. An item in a hand, in a frame or on a stand is not catch. So **don't litter near a camp**.

2235.content: It keeps 4 blocks away from a stranger and hides behind its creel; to kin it comes up and looks.

2236.content:
Hold a thing with the band's craved Spring in your hand — a Snagling comes up and sniffs: you can see the gift is right
without the Loupe.

2237.content:
**The beads on its ears** and the Charmer's pod glow in the band's craving color, and the Loupe writes "The band craves …" under the
name — even before it is read.

2238.content: Every band craves one Spring — the one weakest in the currents of the place it was born.

2239.content: See the craving: the bead color or the Loupe line.

2240.content:
Bring **gifts to the craving**. A gift is worth the amount of the craved Spring in the item's currents, as the Loupe reads
them, for the whole stack: cod has  2, coal  3, cobblestone  2,
bamboo  1. Compound currents do not count — look at the Spring's own rune.

2241.content:
Drop the item nearby — it gets picked up and counts for you. Or hand a stack over with a right-click: from your hands
a Snagling takes only what carries the craving, anything else it sniffs and turns away from. From the ground it takes
everything — without craving, silently, with a snort.

2242.content:
**The measure is 32 craving per band**: 16 cobblestone for a Strata band, 11 coal for an Ember band, 32 bamboo for a Gale band.
Until it is full, a mod line tells you how much you have brought.

2243.content:
When you are accepted, the band calls you kin: everyone within 32 blocks jumps and claps, knots of the craving color tie
above you, and everything the Snaglings took from you and still carry spills at your feet. The first time, the band gives you
a : while you carry it, new bands need half the gifts. Kin is for good — until you hit a Snagling of
that band yourself.

2244.content:
Hit a Snagling (by hand, projectile, lens), kill one, or open or break the Catch Heap as a stranger — and the whole band within
32 blocks holds a grudge: for **10 minutes**, for a kill **20**, and the gift measure doubles. The grudge survives leaving and
restarting; gifts lift it — a band accepts them even while it holds a grudge. A band never touches its kin.

2245.content: A band with a grudge attacks, and each kin has its own move — and its own answer:

A killed Snagling drops its whole creel and cord, a Gleaner sometimes a , a Charmer a

For kin a right-click opens trading; a stranger gets the line "bring a gift to their craving". There are no levels: each
Snagling has 4–5 trades, small stock that refills by dawn — "the river brought it". Every trade asks for things with the band's
craved Spring (a Tide band — fish, kelp; an Ember band — coal; a Strata band — cobblestone, deepslate; a Gale band — feathers,
bamboo) and gives the wares of its kin:

**Gleaner** — the river's catch: , concentrates, , glint wisps,

2252.content:

2253.content:

2254.content:
A ware worth more than half its price in the band's craving is never sold to that band — you can't hand it back as a gift for
more than you paid.

2255.content:
The  opens like a chest for kin: "what flows belongs to no one", take what you like. For a stranger
the first click says "The band is watching you", the second, 3 seconds later, opens it — and the band holds a grudge.
A  is untied by using it — one thing the river brought falls out.  can be
thrown by players too: 4 seconds on a monster.

2256.content:
The **Snagling Peddler** is the only one of the folk who trades with strangers, with no gifts needed. He walks upstream from
camp to camp under a creel taller than himself, in a wide straw hat, with a staff, and behind him on a lead comes a laden
Driftback.

2257.content:
**When**: the Peddler's Visit event — for those who have studied : the first one in a day or two, then
every 3–5 days, by day. He comes out 18–32 blocks from a player near the surface (no deeper than 8 blocks underground and not
into a murky chunk), bows with his hat and stands as a stall by where he came out for **one game day**, then shoulders his
creel and slips away into the reeds. Turning off the game's wandering traders with the world rule turns him off too.

2258.content:
**Payment** — things with his craved Spring (the weakest Spring of the place where he came out; the Loupe writes it under his
name). With a  in your inventory — **half price**. He takes no emeralds.

2259.content:
**Wares** — per visit: one **map** with a red cross to a ruin (a Snagling Camp, a Reckoner Lock or a Fallen Gauge Stone —
untouched), one rare **find** (a ,  or two Catch Bundles) and four
**wares** — saplings and herbs of faraway places. The stock does not refill.

2260.content: Hit him and he takes offense, closes the trade and vanishes. He drops only cord: no wares are carried on his body.

2261.content: World events — the Peddler's Visit and other Omens, cult raids.

2262.content: The Bower — the world inside a skein, the first of the worlds on a fluxionist's path.

2263.content: Folk reference — every trade of the kins and the Peddler.

2324.content:
A **cameo** () is a ready piece of tracery on a small blank: instead of springs it has an Inlet, where the bigger board's
stream enters, and an Outlet, where it leaves. A lens blank has one cameo socket, a great one two; the Pantograph copies the drawing, the

2325.content:

the blank's facets — it will not be cut.

2326.content:

again.

2327.content:

by a Snarl Thread. Recutting a lens costs again.

2328.content: A tracery costs more than the same strength from the Lens Grinder: it buys precision and invention, not endless damage.

2339.content: The way in: the Sluice Arch

2349.content:
**The Stillness** is the world of the Great Stilling worked by the Order of the Still Hour. The sun stands at the horizon — the very
Still Hour; water is glass, fire is cold light, dust and drops hang in the air, people froze mid-step. You come here for things found
nowhere else: **Still Grains** and **stillmetal**, **Freshet Ore**, the Order's gear, the Hubstones of guardians and masters — and the
**Heart of the Stilling**, the key to the finale. The Codex entry is .

2350.content:
The worlds come in order: you reach the Stillness after the Lees and the Quickstream.
The Stillness entry opens once you have passed through an arch into the Quickstream and read a **Gauge Ring** with the Loupe — an arch
once stood in its middle.

2351.content: The way in is the same **Sluice Arch** that leads to the Quickstream: flux pays the way there, stillness pays it here.

2352.content:
Build a frame 4 × 5 of  (corners as you like) and leave the 2 × 3 opening empty. The frame plan and
"Place a ghost" are on the second page of the entry.

2353.content:
Keep **three**  in your inventory and throw a pinch of  on the frame: the
grains and the dust are spent, and the opening is veiled with stilled air.

2354.content:
Step into the veil and stay for four seconds: the world around you freezes, turns white and falls silent — and you are there. On the
other side an arch of stillstone bricks waits for you; stand in its veil the same way to return to your own. You can step into a veil
a friend has woken, so two can go together.

2355.content: The first arrival is a reading for the Codex and Deep Dissonance 3 (guide: Dissonance).

2356.content:
**Where to get grains before the Stillness**: an untangled Snarl and the Seine give them up, and they lie in the chests of the Chapels
of the Still in the ordinary world (guide: Ruins and dungeons). Grains found earlier wait for the entry:
without it the arch to the Stillness stays cold.

2357.content:
**There is no flux**: flux and riverbed are zero. The , devices and the Flux Workbench are silent without a
store of their own. Only what lies in a Thaw Lantern's circle flows.

2358.content:
**Nothing flows**: seas and rivers are  (solid glass, no bucket takes it), fire is
 (light without heat), there is no lava, the clouds stand, there is no weather.

2359.content: **You cannot sleep**, set a spawn point or use a respawn anchor. There are no raids or patrols.

2360.content:
**The Living Minute**: every 30–45 minutes, for whoever stands outside a lantern's circle, the Stillness moves for a minute —
riverbed 16, still Skeins thaw, Sentinels wake, grains fall from the sky. More in World events.

2361.content: An Iris shader pack is not applied in the Stillness: it would sway leaves in the wind and ripple the water, and here nothing moves.

2362.content:
The  is your light in the Stillness: in its circle everything flows again. It is made at the Flux
Workbench; the entry is .

2363.content:
A current shard burns in its cradle: a primal shard for a minute, an Ember shard for two; the cradle holds up to four minutes. Use
the lantern with an empty hand to see how long it will still burn.

2364.content:
While it burns, **for eight blocks around** water pours, fire burns out, hanging dust settles, Grain Drifts fall as grains, and
Stilled Figures finish their step: some crumble into rime, leaving a , others walk on as Laggards.
When the lantern goes out, the circle stills again.

2365.content: A  broken in the circle gives not grains but .

2366.content: **Quickwater** from the Quickstream, poured out in the Stillness, thaws a circle of 3 blocks for a minute — a short thaw on the go.

2367.content:
**Guard the lantern from Rime Moths** (). These moths of hoarfrost hang in the air, frozen in flight; the
warmth of a lit lantern wakes them from 24 steps away. A moth settles on the lantern and drinks its store: three moths drink a shard's
minute in ten seconds. It is fragile — strike it down near the lantern and the warmth goes back. The **Salamander** of the Halted
Blaze is the lantern's friend: in the circle it thaws, lies down beside it and breathes into it (the lantern burns longer), snaps up
Rime Moths, then rests for ten minutes.

A totem is a carved post that **holds a law on a place**: inside its circle something never happens (a creeper doesn't explode,
fire doesn't spread, an enderman doesn't teleport) or something always does (a sprout grows even in the dark). The totem does
nothing by itself — it snuffs the forbidden event the moment it happens and pays for that with the flux of its chunk. Codex
entries — , , ,  and

2455.content:
Three trades of  live in river villages near the flux of the world: the **lamplighter**, the **gauger** and the
**herbalist**. They are ordinary game villagers with a profession of their own — trading, levels, beds and curing a zombie
villager all work as usual. They sell what a fluxionist needs early: opaline, Knotted Cords and Reckoner Records, current
shards, saplings, Fisher's Chowder and float lanterns. Codex entry — : reading a villager's
workplace with the Loupe opens it. Every trade by level is in the villagers reference.

2456.content:
The mod's **houses** stand in game villages — plains, desert, savanna, snowy and taiga: the lamplighter's house, the
gauger's tower and the herbalist's house. About half of all villages have one, usually just one. You can tell it from the
street: by the porch stands a lantern on a lumenash or willow post, and each trade has its own mark — float lanterns on the
water of the yard pool, a full-height clepsydra in the window, current herbs in the hothouse.

2457.content:
You can also **make your own villager**: place a Wax Kettle, a Clepsydra or a Herb Mortar next to an unemployed villager —
he takes the workplace and learns the trade. Workplaces are crafted on a plain crafting table, no Codex entries needed.

gauger a felt cap with a brass ring and a measuring cord across the chest, the herbalist a kerchief with a sprig of herbs and
a glowing vial of tonic.

2491.content: is a large magic mod for Minecraft 26.3 and 1.21.1 on Fabric and NeoForge with its own lore and its own mechanics.

2492.content:
Stone is a current that slowed over eons; wood flows over years, flesh over days, fire in an instant. The measure of how fast
and by what a thing changes is its **flux**. Whoever can read the flux sees the world not as things but as streams: 
runs in stone,  in fire; a river's flux is alive, an abandoned mine's is stagnant. The art of reading and
guiding flux is **fluxion**, and its master is a **fluxionist**.

2493.content:
The **Reckoners**, an ancient order that first measured the currents of the world, left behind Gauge Stones, locks on old riverbeds
and scraps of their records. Part of the order decided that perfection lies in stillness and carried out the **Great Stilling**:
part of the world froze whole. So the **Stillness** came to be — a world where nothing flows.

2494.content:
Flux that has nowhere to flow does not vanish — it stagnates. Stagnant flux is **murk**: it gathers wherever a fluxionist takes
flux roughly, and it settles. Settled murk becomes **mire** — a living blight that creeps over the land and grows creatures.

2495.content:
You are a new fluxionist. Your book is the : your own notebook, where you record what you read
in the world.

2496.content:
**Reading and knowledge.** The  reads the currents of any block, thing, creature and the open sky; every
first reading brings notes to the Codex. The Codex holds entries by chapter and the **Wheel of forty-two currents**.

2497.content:
**Alchemy.** The  dissolves things into a distillate of currents and brews new things from it — heat,
catalysts and murk you have to deal with. Vessels and siphons carry the distillate further.

2498.content:
**Artifice and devices.** The  crafts with the flux of your chunk; dozens of devices run on flux.
The  is a bracer you pour flux through, with lenses. **Confluence** pours currents into a thing on an altar.

2499.content: **Skeins of living light** hang in the world: you draw threads from them, and a dense skein can be opened and entered — your own Bower.

2500.content:
**Worlds.** Atmospheric biomes of the Overworld, the Stillness, the Lees, the Quickstream and the Meanders, three cults and their
guardians — and a finale that changes your world for good.

2517.content:
Put the mod file for your game version and loader into the `mods` folder together with **GeckoLib** and **TerraBlender**
(on Fabric, also **Fabric API**). The file name says both: `…-fabric-1.21.1-….jar`, `…-neoforge-26.3-….jar`. Take the
libraries for the same version and loader: a NeoForge file will not start on Fabric, a 26.3 file will not start on 1.21.1,
and the other way round. A world cannot move between 26.3 and 1.21.1.

2519.content:
Minecraft 1.21.1 lacks some things from newer versions of the game that  relies on, so the mod adds them there itself, with
the same names and the same use: pale oak and poplar (logs, planks, doors, trapdoors, leaves, saplings — the poplar grows in
autumn yellow, orange or red), short and tall dry grass, the pale moss block, pale moss carpet and pale hanging moss, the copper
nugget, copper tools, copper armor and copper horse armor. In survival you find them where the newer versions put them: poplars
grow in the Dappled Forest, pale oak with pale and hanging moss in the Pale Garden (on 1.21.1  adds these two biomes, and
they generate where they do in 26.3: the Dappled Forest on cool dry plains, the Pale Garden on humid dark forest plateaus), dry
grass in deserts and badlands, copper horse armor lies in the chests of dungeons, temples, fortresses, End cities and village
weaponsmiths, and the wandering trader sells the saplings, logs, moss and dry grass. They also grow from bone meal, appear in the mod's structures and places, and are crafted and smelted as in the
newer versions; you find them in the  tabs. In Minecraft 26.3 the mod has none of these — the game's own things are used
there.

2677.content:
With a shader pack (Iris) the mod draws its screen effects as light layers, and its own shaders in the world and its signs in
the sky around the shader pack: that way they look as intended. **Ignore shaders** is **at your own risk**: the mod draws everything
as it does without a shader pack — screen effects of strong moments, its own shaders in the world, signs in the sky. The shader
pack does not know these drawings, so some may look wrong (neon instead of brass, dark or bright patches), but the game won't
crash because of it.

2678.content:
The toggle is in the mod settings, below the graphics cards; it shows only when Iris (or Oculus) is installed. Turning it on
asks for a confirmation, turning it off is instant; no restart is needed. Off by default.

2679.content: On the mod's page in Sodium's settings there is an "Ignore shaders…" button: it opens the mod settings with the same question.

2680.content:
If the shader pack refuses one of the mod's drawings, the mod goes back to light layers by itself until the game restarts,
and the toggle says "off: shaders refused it".

2681.content:
The mod's own worlds where shader packs do not apply at all (the Lees, the Stillness, the Quickstream, the Bower) are not
changed by the toggle: everything there is already drawn as without a shader pack.

2705.content:
Hold the Loupe on a thing, a block, a creature or the open air: after a second and a half it reads the target and shows its currents.
Every new thing you read gives **notes** by chapter, and a current you have never met before is **revealed**. When an entry has
enough knowledge, press Study in the Codex — the entry opens fully, and the next ones show through behind it.

2712.content:
Flux taken roughly settles as **murk**: in smelting it down, in a failed confluence, in a cheap lens. Settled murk becomes **mire** —
a living blight that creeps over the land. The entry  tells about it.
